The current HIV testing coordinator and case manager are individuals who were previously clients of the program, demonstrating a model of empowerment and leadership development within the community. 2. Streetwise and Safe (SAS) is an organization that focuses on building leadership, skills, knowledge, and community among LGBTQ youth of color aged 16 to 24 who face criminalization, including those involved in or perceived to be involved in sex work. 3. Many of these young individuals have experienced homelessness or are currently homeless, and some have engaged in sex work to meet their basic survival needs. 4. SAS youth leaders conduct tailored know your rights workshops for LGBTQ youth, providing critical information about their legal rights and strategies to enhance safety and reduce harm during interactions with law enforcement and the judicial system. 5. SAS creates opportunities for youth to engage in policy discussions, advocate for themselves, and collectively act to protect their rights. 6. SAS has been at the forefront of campaigns to end discriminatory practices such as stop and frisk and other forms of police misconduct. 7. SAS youth have testified before local and state governments, successfully advocating for changes to the New York City Police Department Patrol Guide to address violations of the rights of transgender and gender non-conforming individuals. 8. SAS is currently part of the Access to Condoms Coalition, campaigning to end the use of condoms as evidence in cases related to sex work under New York Penal Law. 9. Police sometimes confiscate condoms found during stop-and-frisk encounters or use them as evidence in sex work or trafficking charges, disproportionately affecting homeless youth or those without stable housing. 10. Due to SAS advocacy, the New York City Police Department announced in May 2014 that it would discontinue using condoms as evidence in certain offenses, though SAS continues to push for broader policy changes. 11. Community Liaison Officers (CLOs) were selected from previously unreached networks and trained on HIV, health information, and services. They used social media and smartphones to reach men who had not been contacted by peer educators before. 12. In Accra, 82% of men reached through this approach had no prior contact with peer educators, while in Kumasi, 66% had never been reached by any intervention. 13. CLOs in Accra identified previously unknown male sex worker brothels and networks, highlighting the importance of social media in reaching hidden populations. 14. The Centre for the Development of People (CEDEP) in Malawi addresses the needs of marginalized populations, particularly men who have sex with men (MSM), in a context of homophobia and criminalization. 15. CEDEP peer educators use snowballing techniques to identify and mobilize MSM, improving access to HIV services and reducing stigma through sensitization of health service providers. 16. CEDEP has trained 80 peer educators, leading to greater mobilization of hidden populations and increased partnerships with health services. 17. Many individuals from key populations experience self-stigma, internalizing societal prejudices, which can lead to shame, loss of self-esteem, and even thoughts of self-harm or suicide. 18. CEDEP-facilitated focus groups have empowered MSM to demand information and services tailored to their needs, such as condom-compatible lubricants. 19. The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIER) in Nigeria focuses on reducing the impact of HIV on MSM and their families through advocacy, communication, and capacity building. 20. TIER’s Integrated MARPs HIV Prevention Programme (IMHIPP) provides HIV prevention, care, and support services in a legally constrained environment, using peer educators and referrals to sensitive service providers. 21. IMHIPP-trained providers deliver palliative care for MSM with AIDS-related illnesses and offer accompanied visits to health facilities for those uncomfortable seeking services alone. 22. The Positive Life program in Russia offers individual counseling via phone, social media, and Skype to young MSM living with HIV, addressing fears of public identification of their sexual orientation or HIV status. 23. Peer counselors provide information on sexuality, safe sex, STIs, ART adherence, and disclosure of HIV status to sexual partners, while also encouraging visits to project offices or trained medical specialists. 24. The Health4Men project in South Africa institutionalizes competence in serving MSM within public clinics through sensitization, medical training, mentoring, and ongoing technical support. 25. Health4Men has established Centers of Excellence in Cape Town and Johannesburg, supported by satellite clinics, to provide services for MSM and stimulate demand through outreach activities. 26. The MOSAIC Men’s Health Initiative in South Africa increases access to HIV prevention services for MSM by supporting peer-led outreach and community-based activities, while sensitizing healthcare workers to MSM-specific needs. 27. Peer outreach workers and clinicians are trained on evidence-based HIV prevention interventions, including post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), to address MSM-related health issues effectively.
